slides.1.title: The Four Main Types of Port
slides.1.items.0.desc: Young and deep red. Blackberry and blueberry fruit with noticeable sweetness, usually aged for about 2–3 years in tanks or large vats without oxidation. The most basic type of Port
slides.1.items.1.desc: Aged oxidatively for many years in small oak casks, turning brown-orange-gold. Nutty, toffee and orange peel aromas. Can carry an age statement of 10/20/30/40 years
slides.1.items.2.desc: A single vintage, bottled after 4-6 years in cask. Sits between Ruby and Vintage, and is the best-value vintage Port
slides.1.items.3.desc: The finest. Produced only in exceptional declared years and bottled after about 2 years in cask (2.5 at most), then ageing a further 20-50 years in bottle. The world's best fortified wine
slides.2.title: Tawny Age Statements: 10/20/30/40 Years
slides.2.html:
The age statement on a Tawny Port (10/20/30/40 years) does not refer to a specific vintage, but to the average age of the wines in the blend.

Label Average cask age Colour Main aromas
10 years 7–15 years Deep amber-orange Orange peel, almond
20 years 17–25 years Golden brown Toffee, nuts
30 years 27–35 years Pale amber-gold Roasted coffee, dried fruit
40 years 35+ years Very pale golden yellow Rum, chocolate, woody notes

Colheita = a single-vintage Tawny, aged in cask for at least 7 years, labelled with the actual harvest year.
slides.3.question: After how many years in cask is Vintage Port usually bottled?
slides.3.explanation: Vintage Port spends only about 2 years in oak (2.5 at most, a short time) before bottling, then continues to age in bottle for a long time. This is because the complexity of Vintage Port comes mainly from bottle ageing, not cask ageing.
slides.4.title: Porto DOC Map
slides.4.description: The Port demarcated region, which overlaps heavily with the Douro, is the only legal source of the world's most famous fortified sweet wine
